::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
The five object types that every Earth Engine script is built from, and the single most important technique on the platform: mapping a function over a collection instead of looping.
:::

## Five containers

Everything in Earth Engine is one of five things. Learning what each holds, and which methods it accepts, converts most of the API from memorisation into deduction.

| Object | Holds | Everyday analogy |
|--------|-------|------------------|
| `ee.Image` | A raster with one or more bands | One photograph |
| `ee.ImageCollection` | An ordered stack of images | A time lapse album |
| `ee.Geometry` | Pure shape: point, line, polygon | A pencil outline on tracing paper |
| `ee.Feature` | A geometry plus attributes | That outline with a label attached |
| `ee.FeatureCollection` | Many features | An attribute table with shapes |

: The Earth Engine type system in full {.striped}

The distinction between `ee.Geometry` and `ee.Feature` is worth pausing on, because it causes recurring confusion. A geometry is only a shape. A feature is a shape carrying properties, which is what lets a training polygon say "this area is mangrove". When Chapter [-@sec-sampling] assigns a `landcover` property to sample points, it is turning geometries into features so that a classifier has something to learn from.

## Bands, and why band names matter so much

An `ee.Image` is not a picture. It is a stack of co registered numeric grids called bands, each holding a different measurement of the same ground.

A Sentinel-2 image carries thirteen spectral bands plus quality layers. A single band image such as SRTM carries one. A classification output carries one, usually named `classification`. A composite you have built might carry twenty five: the original reflectance bands, several indices, radar backscatter, elevation, slope and texture measures.

Select a band by name, never by position:

```javascript
var nearInfrared = image.select('B8');            // one band
var visible = image.select(['B4', 'B3', 'B2']);   // three, in that order
var allSpectral = image.select('B.*');            // regular expression
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common failure: silent band name changes
Operations rename bands, and the new names are not always what you expect.
`normalizedDifference()` produces a band called `nd` unless you `.rename()` it.
`reduce(ee.Reducer.median())` appends `_median` to every band name, while the
shorthand `.median()` leaves names unchanged. Mixing the two forms in one
script produces layers that refuse to draw, with an error naming a band you
are certain you created. When that happens, `print(image.bandNames())` first.
:::

## Why `for` loops fail here

This is the central technique of the platform, and the point where programmers with existing experience most often go wrong.

Consider adding NDVI to every image in a year of Sentinel-2 data, roughly seventy scenes. The instinct from ordinary programming is a loop.

```javascript
// Do not do this.
var imageList = collection.toList(collection.size());
var results = [];
for (var i = 0; i < 70; i++) {
  var image = ee.Image(imageList.get(i));
  results.push(addNdvi(image));
}
```

Every iteration of that loop runs in your browser. Each one issues a separate request, waits for a reply, and only then proceeds. Seventy sequential round trips is slow at best, and on a real collection of several thousand scenes the browser stops responding entirely. Worse, `collection.size()` is a server value, so the loop bound has to be pulled to the client with `getInfo()`, which blocks everything until it returns.

The server side equivalent is one line.

```javascript
var results = collection.map(addNdvi);
```

That expresses the same intent as a single instruction. Google's planner distributes it across as many machines as the work requires, and they run at the same time rather than one after another. Nothing returns to your browser until you ask for a result.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-map-vs-loop
%%| fig-cap: "The same work, arranged two ways. The loop is bounded by round trip latency; the map is bounded only by how many machines are free."
flowchart TB
    subgraph loop["for loop (client side, sequential)"]
        direction LR
        L1["scene 1"] --> L2["scene 2"] --> L3["scene 3"] --> LN["... scene 70"]
    end
    subgraph mapped["map (server side, parallel)"]
        direction LR
        M0["one instruction"]
        M0 --> M1["scene 1"]
        M0 --> M2["scene 2"]
        M0 --> M3["scene 3"]
        M0 --> MN["... scene 70"]
    end
```

### The rules of a mappable function

A function passed to `.map()` runs on the server, which imposes three constraints.

It must accept exactly one argument and return exactly one object of the same type it received. An image in, an image out.

It cannot use `print()`, `Map.addLayer()` or `getInfo()`. Those are client operations and there is no client where the function is running. This is a frequent surprise: debugging inside a mapped function requires returning diagnostic values as properties, then printing the collection afterwards.

It cannot use JavaScript `if` statements on server values. Use `ee.Algorithms.If()`, or restructure so the branch is not needed, which is usually possible and usually cleaner.

## Reducers: collapsing a stack

`.map()` transforms a collection into another collection of the same length. A **reducer** collapses many values into fewer, and it works along whichever axis you point it at.

Along **time**, a reducer turns a stack of images into one image. This is compositing, and Chapter [-@sec-cloud] uses it heavily.

```javascript
var annual = collection.median();       // one image, per pixel median
```

Along **space**, a reducer turns an image into statistics over a region.

```javascript
var meanNdvi = image.reduceRegion({
  reducer: ee.Reducer.mean(),
  geometry: studyArea,
  scale: 10,           // metres. A scientific choice, not a speed setting.
  maxPixels: 1e9       // raise the safety ceiling for large areas
});
```

Along **bands**, a reducer combines several measurements at one location, which is how the ensemble vote in Chapter [-@sec-supervised] works.

::: {.callout-important}
## Scientific integrity: `scale` is an analytical decision
`reduceRegion` requires a `scale`, and the number you pass changes the answer. Computing mangrove area at 10 metres captures narrow fringing stands that disappear at 100 metres. Neither figure is wrong. Choose the scale that matches the feature size you are reporting on, state it, and use it consistently across every year of a time series. A change in scale between years will manifest as an apparent change on the ground.
:::

## Putting the pieces together

Almost every workflow in this book has the same skeleton, and recognising it makes new scripts easier to read.

```javascript
// 1. Define where and when.
var aoi = ee.Geometry.Point([117.58, -0.84]);

// 2. Filter a collection down to what is relevant.
var collection = ee.ImageCollection('COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED')
  .filterBounds(aoi)
  .filterDate('2023-01-01', '2023-12-31');

// 3. Map a per image function across it.
var processed = collection.map(maskCloudsAndAddIndices);

// 4. Reduce the stack to a single analysis ready image.
var composite = processed.median().clip(aoi);

// 5. Do something with the result: classify, chart, or export.
Map.addLayer(composite, visualisation, 'Composite');
```

Filter, map, reduce, act. Chapter [-@sec-cloud] fills that skeleton in completely.

## On a real reservoir: Jatiluhur, 2014 to 2024

Everything above, on one real place. Jatiluhur is the reservoir that supplies much of Jakarta's water. The script maps an index over every Landsat image, reduces a year three different ways, and then turns a water mask into one number per dry season. Read the two maps side by side before the chart: the median and the greenest pixel are both "the 2019 image", and they do not agree.

## Many regions at once: fire in Riau

reduceRegion answers one question about one area. reduceRegions answers it for every feature in a collection, in one call. This listing from the GEE101 fire exercise counts a decade of confident fire detections in each of Riau's twelve districts, and then does the same for the whole province one year at a time.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Write a function that adds a band holding the acquisition year of each image, and map it over a collection. Hint: `image.date().get('year')` and `ee.Image.constant()`.
2. Take the loop above and rewrite it with `.map()`. Time both if you have the patience, and note where the loop stops being merely slow and becomes unusable.
3. Compute the mean elevation of your study area at 30 metres and at 300 metres. Explain the difference in one sentence.
4. Deliberately write a mapped function with no `return` statement and read the error. It is not obvious, and recognising it once is worth the exercise.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

**1.** ```javascript
var addYear = function (image) {
  var year = image.date().get('year');
  return image.addBands(ee.Image.constant(year).rename('year').toInt16());
};
var withYear = collection.map(addYear);
print(withYear.first().bandNames());   // includes 'year'
```
`ee.Image.constant` accepts the server-side number directly, so no `getInfo()` is needed. Casting to an integer keeps the band small.

**2.** ```javascript
var results = collection.map(addNdvi);
```
The loop issues one request per image and waits for each; with tens of images it is slow, and once the collection runs to hundreds or thousands (and `size().getInfo()` blocks before the loop starts) the browser stops responding. The mapped version returns immediately, because nothing is computed until you display or export it.

**3.** Expect the 300 m mean to differ by a few metres or less in gentle terrain and by more in steep terrain. At 300 m each value is computed from a coarser pyramid level, so valleys and peaks are averaged together and pixels on the boundary are counted differently. One sentence: "The mean changes because the scale changes which pixels, and how many, enter the average; the scale is part of the result."

**4.** Earth Engine reports `User-defined methods must return a value.`, often from a line far from the function itself. The fix is simply `return image.addBands(...)`. Whenever a `.map()` fails mysteriously, check the `return` first.
:::
